tribe: An-Namir ibn Qasit of Rabi'a — of Mosul
teaser: Quraysh told him he could keep his life or his fortune. He asked them to confirm the terms, then paid.
quran_mention: Reported to have been revealed about him — Quran 2:207

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: An Arab boy who grew up speaking Greek
layers.content:
He was Suhayb ibn Sinan, and his lineage runs through an-Namir ibn Qasit back to Rabi'a — as Arab as anyone in Makka. His people's houses were in Mosul, or by some reports in a town on the bank of the Euphrates between Jazira and Mosul. His father, or his uncle, was a governor for Khosrau over Ubulla. This was a family with standing in the Persian administration.

Then the Greeks raided that area and took Suhayb, who was a young child. Ibn Sa'd preserves the sound his uncle made when he heard: 'I ask Allah! The Namiri boy, and his family in ath-Thani.'

He grew up among the Greeks and lost his language. Men of Kalb later bought him and brought him to Makka, where Abdullah ibn Jud'an at-Taymi bought him and set him free. His own family and his son told it differently — that he escaped the Greeks as an adult and came to Makka of his own accord and made a formal alliance with Ibn Jud'an. Ibn Sa'd records both.

He was a very reddish man, neither tall nor short but inclined to shortness, with a great deal of hair, and he dyed it with henna. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the kunya Abu Yahya.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Two strangers at a door, each afraid to say why
layers.content:
The scene is one of the best in the whole early record, and Ammar ibn Yasir tells it.

'I met Suhayb ibn Sinan at the door of the house of al-Arqam while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was there. I asked him, what do you want? He asked me, what do you want? I replied, I want to visit Muhammad and hear his words. He said, that is what I want.'

Neither would go first. Each had come alone, each had calculated the risk of being seen, and each was waiting for the other to incriminate himself. Then one of them said it out loud, and the standoff collapsed into company.

They went in together. Islam was offered to them and they accepted. They spent the day there and left in the evening, still concealing it. Ibn Sa'd notes they became Muslim after about thirty men had done so.

Al-Hasan transmits that the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Suhayb was the first of the Greeks' — the first from the Byzantine world to enter Islam, the opening of a door that would eventually take in nations.

And then Urwa ibn az-Zubayr's line, which follows almost every early name in this book: Suhayb was one of the victimised believers who were tortured for Allah in Makka.
layers.hadith_ref: 'Suhayb was the first of the Greeks' — reported from al-Hasan through Yunus, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (Ammar ibn Yasir via Abu Ubayda; Urwa ibn az-Zubayr)

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Sore eyes, fresh dates, and a joke that landed
layers.content:
Khuzayma ibn Thabit says the last two people to emigrate to Madinah were Ali and Suhayb ibn Sinan, in the middle of Rabi' al-Awwal. He arrived last, hungry, and with ophthalmia from the road.

The Prophet ﷺ was at Quba with Abu Bakr and Umar, and in front of them were fresh dates that Kulthum ibn al-Hidm had brought. Suhayb went straight into the dates. Umar said, 'Messenger of Allah, do you not see Suhayb eating fresh dates when he is suffering from ophthalmia?' The Prophet ﷺ turned to him: 'You eat fresh dates when you are suffering from ophthalmia?' Suhayb said, 'I eat them for the half of my sound eye.' The Prophet ﷺ smiled.

He then complained to Abu Bakr that he had been promised company on the road and been left behind — and said his only provision the whole way had been a mudd of flour he kneaded at al-Abwa.

In Madinah he lodged with Sa'd ibn Khaythama, where the unmarried men stayed. The Prophet ﷺ made brotherhood between him and al-Harith ibn as-Simma. He was at Badr, Uhud, the Ditch and every expedition. In later years he would say to people: come, and we will tell you about our battles.
layers.hadith_ref: Reported from Umar ibn al-Hakam through Abd al-Hakim ibn Suhayb — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (Khuzayma ibn Thabit; Umar ibn al-Hakam; Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatada)

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: They wanted the money. He said, take it.
layers.content:
Quraysh had a specific objection to him leaving. Abu Uthman an-Nahdi's report gives their words: 'You came to us here poor and despicable, and you increased your money with us and reached what you reached, and now you take your person and your wealth. By Allah, that will not happen.'

He answered with a question rather than an argument. 'If I leave my wealth, will you let me go?' They said yes. He gave them all his property. The Prophet ﷺ heard and said, 'Suhayb is profitable. Suhayb is profitable.'

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab's version has the confrontation on the road. Quraysh followed him and he dismounted, took what was in his quiver, and said: company of Quraysh, you know I am the best archer among you. By Allah, you will not reach me until I have shot every arrow in this quiver and then struck you with my sword until nothing is left in my hands. Do what you want. If you wish, I will direct you to my wealth and you let me go. They said yes.

A third account has him say to the Prophet ﷺ: Quraysh took me and imprisoned me, so I purchased myself and my family for my wealth. The details differ. The transaction does not.

It is reported that Quran 2:207 was revealed about this. Ibn Sa'd transmits that connection from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab; report it as reported.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 2:207 — «وَمِنَ النَّاسِ مَن يَشْرِي نَفْسَهُ ابْتِغَاءَ مَرْضَاتِ اللَّهِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ رَءُوفٌ بِالْعِبَادِ» — 'And among people is one who sells his own self seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah is Most Kind to His slaves'
layers.hadith_ref: 'A profitable sale, Abu Yahya' — reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and from Abu Uthman an-Nahdi, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (Abu Uthman an-Nahdi; Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab; Umar ibn al-Hakam)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Umar questioned three things about him. He answered all three.
layers.content:
Umar once put it to him directly, and it is worth reading as three separate accusations. Suhayb, why are you called Abu Yahya when you have no child? You say you are one of the Arabs when you are a Greek man. And you feed people a great deal, which is extravagance with wealth.

Suhayb took them in order. The kunya: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave it to me. The lineage: I am a man from an-Namir ibn Qasit of the people of Mosul, but I was captured by the Greeks as a young boy — after I already knew my family and my people and my lineage. The feeding: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, the best of you is the one who feeds people and returns the greeting. That is what made me feed people.

A man taken as a child, sold twice, tortured, and stripped of a fortune, holding on to the exact record of who he was.

Umar trusted him at the end. In his final instructions to the Council he said: let Suhayb lead you in the prayer. When Umar died, the Muslims looked to Suhayb, and he led the prescribed prayers by Umar's command, and he prayed the funeral prayer over Umar.

He died in Shawwal 38 AH at the age of seventy, in Madinah, and was buried in al-Baqi'. May Allah be pleased with him. Everything he had was taken from him twice, and he never once agreed to be less than he was.
layers.hadith_ref: 'The best of you is the one who feeds people and returns the greeting' — narrated by Suhayb, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III (Hamza ibn Suhayb from his father)
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: Why was Suhayb called ar-Rumi, 'the Byzantine', when his lineage was Arab?

options.text: His mother was Greek
He was captured by the Greeks as a child and grew up among them
He traded with Byzantium for years
He was born in Constantinople

quiz.scholar_reflection: His people were an-Namir ibn Qasit of Rabi'a, settled near Mosul, and his father or uncle governed Ubulla for Khosrau. The Greeks raided and took him. Muhammad ibn Sirin's report insists on the point: Suhayb was one of the Arabs.

quiz.prompt: How did Suhayb and Ammar ibn Yasir come to enter Islam together?

options.text: They were arrested together and met in prison
Abu Bakr brought them both to the Prophet ﷺ
They met at the door of the house of al-Arqam, each too cautious to say why he had come
They heard the Qur'an recited at the Ka'bah on the same day

quiz.citation: Ammar ibn Yasir's account, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ammar asked what do you want, Suhayb asked him the same, and only when Ammar admitted he wanted to hear Muhammad ﷺ speak did Suhayb say, that is what I want too. They went in together and left in the evening still hiding it.

quiz.prompt: What did Quraysh demand before they would let him leave Makka?

options.text: His entire property
That he leave his family behind
That he renounce Islam publicly first
A guarantor from Banu Hashim

quiz.citation: Abu Uthman an-Nahdi and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Their complaint was that he had arrived poor and grown wealthy among them, so the wealth was theirs. He asked one question — if I leave my wealth, will you let me go — and paid the moment they said yes.

quiz.prompt: What did the Prophet ﷺ say when he heard what the sale had cost him?

options.text: 'Your wealth will be returned to you'
'A profitable sale, Abu Yahya'
'You should have kept a portion'
'Quraysh will answer for this at Badr'

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; the connection with Quran 2:207 is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab
quiz.scholar_reflection: The word used is the language of trade — profit, a good deal. He had been bought and sold as property twice in his life. This time he was the buyer, and what he purchased was himself.

quiz.prompt: What did Umar instruct the Council to do, in his final instructions?

options.text: To send Suhayb as governor to Kufa
To repay Suhayb his lost Makkan wealth
To let Suhayb lead them in the prayer
To consult Suhayb on the Byzantine frontier

quiz.citation: Reported from Amir ibn Abdullah ibn az-Zubayr and from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: It was a caretaker role at the most dangerous moment in the community's politics — a neutral man with no clan stake. He also prayed the funeral prayer over Umar.

quiz.prompt: At the door of al-Arqam neither man would speak first. When have you waited for someone else to say the thing you were already thinking?

options.text: Often. I would rather be second than exposed.
I have missed real chances by waiting
I usually go first and sometimes regret it
It depends entirely on what it would cost me

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ammar ibn Yasir's account of meeting Suhayb, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Two men who wanted the same thing stood in each other's way for as long as it took one of them to be honest. The whole standoff was made of caution, not disagreement.

quiz.prompt: He handed over everything he owned to walk out of Makka. What would you find hardest to leave behind?

options.text: Money and security. I am honest about that.
Standing — what people in my circle think of me
Comfort. Not wealth, just the routine.
I do not know, and I would rather not find out

quiz.citation: Reflection on Quran 2:207 and Suhayb's ransom, Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had built that wealth from nothing, as a freed captive in a city that despised him for it. He gave it away in a single sentence and arrived in Madinah with a handful of flour.

quiz.prompt: Umar challenged his kunya, his lineage and his generosity in one breath. What part of who you are do you find yourself having to defend?

options.text: Where I come from. People decide it for me.
My practice — I am told it is too much or too little
How I spend, and on whom
Nothing. I have stopped explaining myself.

quiz.citation: Reported from Hamza ibn Suhayb from his father, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He did not get defensive and he did not concede. For each charge he produced a source: the Prophet ﷺ gave me this name, I know my own lineage, and the Prophet ﷺ told me to feed people.

quiz.prompt: Sore-eyed and starving, he made a joke about the half of his good eye. What does humour do for you when things are bad?

options.text: It is how I survive things
It feels like avoidance when I do it
I lose my sense of humour first and everything gets worse
I can only joke about it much later

quiz.citation: Reported from Umar ibn al-Hakam, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had just lost a fortune and walked a desert road alone on a measure of flour. His first recorded words in Madinah are a joke, and the Prophet ﷺ smiled at it.

quiz.prompt: He arrived last of all the Muhajirun and was still trusted to lead the prayer at the death of a caliph. What does that say about arriving late?

options.text: That order of arrival is not the measure
It gives me hope about my own late start
He was late by days, not years — I would not compare
Standing came from what he paid, not when he showed up

quiz.citation: Reflection on Khuzayma ibn Thabit's report and Umar's final instructions, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He was the last man in and had no clan in Madinah to speak for him. That was precisely why Umar could hand him the prayer at the most fragile moment the community had faced.
